Chambers of the Alhambra City Hall.

LAND ACKNOWLEDGEMENT: We acknowledge that the land on which we are gathered is the
traditional, ancestral, and unceded territory of the Gabrielino/Tongva peoples. We seek to prioritize

Gabrielino/Tongva people who still consider themselves the caretakers of this land. It is through their

2.  UPDATE ON SUSTAINABILITY PLAN AND DEVELOPMENT OF IMPLEMENTATION
  STRATEGIES – F2M22-64

  The City Council Sustainability Subcommittee consisting of Mayor Pérez and Councilmember
  Maloney met with City staff and Environmental Science Associates (ESA) consultants to
  review outcomes or feedback from existing conditions and Phase 1 community outreach
  efforts. The purpose of the data collection was to gain perspective of priority sustainability
  issues among community members and receive input on the draft sustainability framework
  which efforts focus on green space, food, mobility, energy, water, air quality, sustainability
  culture, green economy, and waste reduction. Community workshops, discussion groups,
  pop-up events, Commission briefings, community questionnaire and social media were
  conducted as part of the early phase of work. Plan development would continue with additional
  outreach to the community, with emphasis on the development of strategies or action items
  for the Council and the community to consider. City Council received an update on the
  Comprehensive Environmental Sustainability Plan, including a summary of outreach highlights
  year to date, and a review of intended talking points with the community to stimulate strategy
  discussions to help the City achieve its targets. Management Analyst MARTEL delivered a
  staff report and Stephanie CARDENA from ESA delivered the presentation, which is on file in
  the City Clerk’s office.

  Public Comment:
  1) Brian OTIS, 320 N. Monterey St., spoke regarding earthquake safety and made further
  suggestions for earthquake safety upgrades to buildings and homes.

  2) Lola ARMENDARIZ made reference to Mr. Otis’s comments and suggested more public
  outreach regarding earthquake safety. She went on to request additional public outreach
  regarding community workshops or sustainability meetings via alternate means and not
  just through digital outreach.

  3) Jennifer NG spoke regarding the need for responsible and less aggressive tree trimming
  to preserve the canopy and public assistance for tree planting on private property.

  4) Shirley TATSUNO, 1408 S. Fifth St., Apt. C, referred to Mr. Otis’s comments regarding
  earthquake retrofits and spoke regarding the high expense to homeowners and property
  owners.

  Discussion: Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER spoke in support of the current work
  done by staff and ESA and suggested publicizing Alhambra’s progress towards sustainability
  in the form of a report card. She referred to Mr. Otis’s comments and highlighted the suggested
  methods to prevent gas leaks.

  Councilmember MALONEY and Ms. CARDENA discussed opportunities for on-road
  2
8-26-24
   transportation in terms of energy reduction. Mr. MALONEY went on to echo Ms. Andrade-
  Stadler’s support for the progress made towards sustainability and continued to speak about
  the City’s participation with Clean Power Alliance. He stressed the need for continued in-depth
  discussion with the Environmental Sustainability Commission to provide feedback and insight.
  Mr. MALONEY and Ms. CARDENA discussed the difference between a Sustainability Plan
  and a Climate Action Plan. They continued to discuss the ability of the Sustainability Plan to
  change with the most current needs of the community and provide adaptability over several
  years within City government operations.

  Councilmember MAZA supported Mr. Maloney’s comments regarding the Sustainability Plan’s
  long-term foundation, referred to Ms. Ng’s comments regarding preserving existing trees, and
  referred to Mr. Otis’s comments regarding earthquake safety measures and state programs
  for earthquake retrofit assistance.

  Vice Mayor LEE supported the programs regarding food sustainability programs, referred to
  the existing Community Garden, supported new community garden opportunities, and
  suggested looking at emergency preparedness programs with regards to emergency food
  supplies.

  Mayor PÉREZ supported the micro forest and community garden programs and requested
  additional information regarding a map of potential sites for both programs. Ms. CARDENA
  discussed the lack of in-ground space and a potential suggestion for rooftop gardens as a
  response. Ms. PÉREZ went on to request a requirement for solar panel installation on public
  buildings; requested additional trees planted in front of City Hall; requested a requirement for
  new commercial or residential buildings to be fully electric or decarbonize, perhaps through
  tax incentives; requested a requirement for the installation of purple air sensors around
  government and school buildings; requested the preservation of existing trees through
  responsible tree trimming and conservation methods; and requested publication of community
  meeting notices in the Around Alhambra and the City Council agendas.

  Ms. PÉREZ further discussed Mr. Otis and Ms. Tatsuno’s comments regarding earthquake
  safety, and requested a future agendized discussion. Ms. LEE stated that she preferred a
  discussion regarding general emergency plans and City Manager BINNQUIST commented on
  the City’s general emergency response plans depending on the specific emergency. City
  Attorney MONTES stated that the plans could be made available to Council. Ms. LEE
  requested specific information be presented to Council at a future meeting; such as command
  centers, communication to residents, emergency response of safety personnel. Ms. PÉREZ
  suggested specifically focusing on earthquake safety plans in terms of the City’s emergency
  preparedness. Council supported the suggestion to agendize a future discussion.

  Action Taken:  City Council received and filed the informational report and direct staff
  as deemed appropriate.

LEE:  Vice Mayor Lee recused herself from the discussion of Item No. 3 as a homeowner in
Alhambra and to avoid any future conflict of interest. City Attorney MONTES clarified that as this
ordinance affected all single-family residences in Alhambra but only specifically those who rented their
property on a short-term basis, there was no known legal reason for Ms. Lee to recuse herself. Ms.
LEE left Council Chambers at 7:47 p.m.

3.  ORDINANCE ADDING CHAPTER 5.92 TO THE ALHAMBRA MUNICIPAL CODE TO
ESTABLISH REGULATIONS FOR SHORT-TERM RENTALS – F2M18-35, F2M24-33,
O2M24-4836
  Code Enforcement Supervisor PEREZ-GARCIA delivered a staff report and presentation
  which is on file in the City Clerk’s office. The City Council identified in the 2024 Strategic Plan
  a goal to develop regulations for short term rentals within the City. Currently, requirements for
  3
8-26-24
   short term rentals included obtaining a business license, a rental license and the only
  regulations applicable were overnight parking standards and noise limits, with no regulations
  to enforce if there are disruptions in the neighborhood. The proposed ordinance would require
  that short term rentals obtain a permit with the City and establishes regulations that property
  owners and tenants of short-term rentals would be required to follow, along with tools for City’s
  enforcement. The regulations would also allow for hosted and non-host short term rentals.
  The short-term rental permit was valid for one year from the date of issuance. The permit was
  non-transferrable and may be renewed annually if certain provisions are met. A registration
  fee would be established at a later date but tied to the hourly rate for staff to process the permit.
  Effective enforcement of non-compliance would be managed by the Code Enforcement
  Division and could involve inspections, issuing notices of violation, administrative citations and
  suspension of permits.

  Public Comment:

  1) Barbara MESSINA, via Zoom, related her negative personal experiences in her
  neighborhood with a short-term rental and a crowded party at the residence. She stated
  that there needed to be greater enforcement of any Short-Term Rental policies to preserve
  local neighborhoods and safe communities.

  2) Katie CHAN spoke regarding the reduction of affordable housing stock due to the
  prevalence of short-term rentals. She proposed a cap on short-term rental permits issued
  annually, stricter enforcement to prevent apartment rentals used as short-term rentals, the
  imposition of a short-term rental tax, issuing zoning restrictions for short-term rentals, and
  for the City to conduct a detailed economic impact study of the effects of short-term rentals.

  3) Noah ABELMAN, via Zoom, supported Ms. Messina’s comments and further discussed
  other short-term rentals in his neighborhood which had drug and alcohol related incidents,
  disruptive parties, and predatory subleasing practices. He also expressed concerns
  regarding private equity and investment firms as well as foreign investors buying single
  family residences as short-term rental properties. He urged Council to revise the ordinance
  to prohibit permits being issued to such owners.

  Public Comment received via email and on file in the City Clerk’s office:

  1) Matthew Buck, Vice President of Public Affairs of California Apartment Association, wrote
  additional suggestions for the Council to consider in the Ordinance.

  2) Noah Suarez-Sikes and Randy Renick, representing Better Neighbors LA, wrote additional
  suggestions for the Council to consider in the Ordinance.

  Discussion: Councilmember MAZA clarified that Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs) were
  not allowed as short-term rentals. He suggested prohibiting short-term rentals in multi-family
  properties and discussed the number of existing short-term rentals in multi-family properties
  with Mr. PEREZ-GARCIA. They continued to discuss other existing short-term rentals, the
  prohibition of permits to subleased tenants or occupants, registering a local contact to respond
  to inquiries or in the event of an emergency, the maximum occupants per bedroom or property,
  and an annual review of the ordinance to address any issues. Mr. MAZA and Director of
  Community Development HO discussed City revenues collected from short-term rentals and
  research into a transit occupancy tax. Mr. MAZA stressed the need for strict enforcement of
  the regulations.

  City Attorney MONTES clarified points regarding enforcement and highlighted the enhanced
  fine schedule as outlined in the ordinance draft. Mr. MAZA suggested a longer suspension of
  future permits due to violations.
  4
8-26-24
   Councilmember MALONEY supported the suggestion to ban multi-unit properties from the
  permits in an effort to preserve housing stock in the City. He referred to comments made by
  Ms. Messina and Mr. Abelman, and suggested on-site inspection of properties prior to
  issuance of a permit. Mr. MALONEY and Mr. HO discussed the map provided of known and
  suspected short-term rentals in the City. Mr. MALONEY supported consideration of a transit
  occupancy tax. He stressed the need for strict enforcement, preventing disruptive renters, and
  longer suspension of permits due to repeated violations.

  Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER supported the suggestion to ban multi-family housing
  properties and further suggested a cap of 500 permits issued. She supported the regulations,
  but stressed the need for strict enforcement. She went on to discuss the prevalence of short-
  term rentals in Alhambra due to the lack of local hotels for vacationers. She suggested the
  permanent revocation of permits for repeat violations. She also supported consideration of a
  transit occupancy tax.

  Mayor PÉREZ agreed with the ban on multi-family housing and suggested one short-term
  rental per natural person to eliminate corporate entities from purchasing housing for temporary
  hotel space. She agreed with Ms. Andrade-Stadler’s suggestion for a cap on permits and a
  permanent revocation of permits for repeat violations. She also supported. Mr. Maloney’s
  suggestion of inspections prior to issuance of a permit as well as the suggestion to consider a
  transit occupancy tax. She suggested discussion of future hotel development in Alhambra to
  further prevent short-term rentals and the purchase of potential housing stock for short-term
  rentals. Ms. PÉREZ also suggested that a community member must be given explicit written
  permission by the property owner to prohibit any circumnavigation of lease agreements.

  Mr. MONTES clarified that staff would research Council’s recommendations and stated that
  due to the number of recommendations, the ordinance would be rewritten and return for
  Council approval at a future meeting. Mr. MONTES listed the recommendations: future
  consideration of a transit occupancy tax ballot measure as a separate agenda item; random
  or periodic inspection of properties as well as upon issuance; a cap of 500 permits; permanent
  revocation of permits; prohibiting non-individual entities from permits; banning short-term
  rentals in multi-family properties; a potential cap of individuals per bedroom; annual review or
  reports of ordinance; and written permission by property owner to a community member. Mr.
  HO clarified that multi-family housing units typically referred to apartments, condominiums,
  duplexes, and triplexes and asked if Council intended to extend the ban to all multi-family
  properties. Ms. PÉREZ stated that she believed that all apartment complexes would be banned
  from permits. Mr. MAZA clarified that properties of five or more units would be banned from
  permits. Mr. MAZA further suggested that a property be owned for a minimum of 12-18 months
  before a permit could be issued. Mr. MONTES stated that a potential negative consequence
  would be that a property owner would buy the home and evict a tenant after a year in order to
  turn it into a short-term rental. Mr. HO clarified several points regarding the overall number of
  short-term rentals and the low number of bad actors. Mr. MAZA suggested the inclusion of an
  inspection fee to assist in allocating staff hours for additional enforcement. Ms. ANDRADE-
  STADLER supported the suggestion of the ban extending to multi-family apartment complexes
  as well as condominium complexes of five or more units.

  Action Taken:  City Council provided direction to staff on changes to the ordinance
  and requested that the ordinance return to Council at a future City Council meeting for
  approval.

4.  AUTHORIZE RFP: ELECTRIC VEHICLE CHARGING STATION INFRASTRUCTURE
AT VARIOUS CITY PARKS – F2M24-56, RFP2M24-17

  The Electric Vehicle (EV) Charging Station Infrastructure project was designed to help the City
  invest in and provide green technology for residents and visitors. This project included the
  installation of up to 18 new EV charging stations in public parking lots at 3 park locations:
  Alhambra Park, Granada Park and the Joslyn Center at Story Park. The proposed EV charging
  stations would be available to the public and enable residents and patrons with electric
  vehicles to charge their cars while visiting the parks. This Request for Proposals (RFP) sought
  to identify a qualified contractor for the deployment of the EV Charging Station Infrastructure
  project.

  Public Comment:  Lola ARMENDARIZ spoke against the EV Charging stations at the
  park locations and specifically Alhambra Park and Joslyn Center due to its heavy use. She
  went on to discuss traffic problems in the City.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council authorized the distribution of a Request for Proposals for
  Electric Vehicle (EV) Charging Station Infrastructure at various City parks; and, directed staff
  to undertake the steps necessary to finalize Council’s action.

  Vote:  Moved:  LEE  Seconded:  MALONEY
  Ayes:  ANDRADE-STADLER, MALONEY, LEE, MAZA, PÉREZ
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

5.  AUTHORIZE RFP: PROFESSIONAL CONSULTANT SERVICES FOR THE
  DEVELOPMENT OF THE FREMONT POCKET PARK PROJECT – F2M24-57,
  RFP2M24-18

  Staff sought professional engineering and design services to provide plans, specifications and
  bid documentation for the Fremont Pocket Park Project. The overall goal of this project was to
  add more green space within the City. The pocket park would include turf, seating, shade
  cover, California native trees, water re-capture features and drought-tolerant plants. The
  project was funded by the State of California Department of Parks and Recreation.

  Public Comment:  Lola ARMENDARIZ spoke against the Fremont proposed pocket park
  and suggested that a police substation would be a better use for the area. She also questioned
  whether residents were notified of this project.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council authorized staff to circulate a Request for Proposals to
  provide design, specifications, and bid documentation for the Fremont Pocket Park Project;
  and, directed staff to undertake the steps necessary to finalize Council’s action.

6.  AUTHORIZE RFP: BANKING SERVICES – F2M24-58, RFP2M24-19

  The City of Alhambra had been banking with Bank of the West for over 20 years until last
  year, when BMO Bank acquired Bank of the West. The City experienced some disruption in
  services following the acquisition. To ensure the City receives the highest level of banking
  services and competitive pricing, staff recommended the distribution of a Request for
  Proposals for banking services.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council authorized the distribution of a Request for Proposals to
  select a qualified bank for comprehensive banking services and competitive pricing to support
  the City’s financial operations with proposals due no later than 11:00 a.m. on October 10, 2024;
  and, directed staff to undertake the steps necessary to finalize Council’s action.

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded: MAZA
  Ayes:  MALONEY, LEE, MAZA, ANDRADE-STADLER, PÉREZ
  Noes:  NONE

7.  AUTHORIZE RFP: INVESTMENT MANAGEMENT AND ADVISORY SERVICES –
  F2M24-58, RFP2M24-20

  The City sought proposals from qualified firms to provide investment services in a
  comprehensive manner to handle the day-to-day administration of the City’s investment
  portfolio and provide discretionary investment advisory services. Staff currently oversaw the
  management of the City’s investment portfolio and proposed the engagement of a consultant
  to enhance the efficiency and expertise applied to this responsibility. The consultant would
  aim to reduce the burden on staff by providing specialized investment management services
  to optimize the City’s investment returns

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council authorized the distribution of a Request for Proposals to
  select a qualified consultant to provide investment management, investment advisory, and
  related services for the City’s investment portfolio with proposals due no later than 11:00 a.m.
  on October 10, 2024; and, direct staff to undertake the steps necessary to finalize Council’s
  action.

  Ayes:  MALONEY, LEE, MAZA, ANDRADE-STADLER, PÉREZ

8.  AWARD CONTRACT: PROFESSIONAL MARKETING AND ADVERTISING SERVICES
IN SUPPORT OF THE CITY’S ORGANIC RECYCLING COLLECTION AND FOOD RECOVERY
PROGRAMS – F2M24-49, RFP2M24-11, C2M24-50, M2M24-139
  7
8-26-24
   On June 24, 2024, the City Council authorized staff to solicit proposals to design the multi-
  media marketing and advertising plan to best disseminate information on SB 1383
  requirements, including how to properly dispose of organic waste. On July 24, 2024, the City
  received 9 proposals from qualified firms. After reviewing the proposals, 4 applicants were
  invited to interview. The City’s selection committee assessed the proposals in accordance with
  the evaluation criteria set forth in the City’s RFP including qualifications, experience,
  references, and capacity. City Fabrick, an environmentally-focused nonprofit organization with
  expertise in community engagement and multilingual marketing, was ranked the highest. City
  Fabrick has strong ties to the San Gabriel Valley, having worked with the City of Monterey
  Park and the SCAG Go Human 2.0 campaign, and has experience in both traditional and
  innovative forms of advertising and outreach with an emphasis on reaching diverse and
  hard-to-reach communities.

  Public Comment:  Shirley TATSUNO spoke regarding the difficulties for apartment
  renters to participate in and comply with the organic recycling program. She suggested more
  outreach, such as a food sorting game booth at the Farmer’s Market, in order to better educate
  and encourage resident participation. She further suggested local school participation.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council awarded a contract, subject to final language approval by
  the City Manager and City Attorney, to City Fabrick in an amount not to exceed $60,000 for
  Professional Marketing and Advertising Services in support of the City’s organics collection
  and food recovery programs in accordance with SB 1383; authorized the City Manager to
  execute the contract; and, directed staff to undertake the steps necessary to finalize the City
  Council’s action. (M2M24-139)

  Vote:  Moved:  LEE  Seconded:  MALONEY
  Ayes:  ANDRADE-STADLER, MALONEY, LEE, MAZA, PÉREZ
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

9.  AWARD CONTRACT PROFESSIONAL CONSULTANT SERVICES FOR THE
  DEVELOPMENT OF THE ALHAMBRA DOG PARK PROJECT AND APPROPRIATION
OF FUNDS FROM THE REGIONAL PARK AND OPEN SPACE DISTRICT, TECHNICAL
  ASSISTANCE FUND – F2M11-36, F2M18-35, RFP2M24-13, C2M24-51, M2M24-140

  On June 24, 2024, the City Council approved the distribution of a Request for Proposals
  (RFP)for professional consultant services for the development of the Alhambra Dog Park
  Project. On July 29, 2024, the City received 4 proposals and 3 firms were invited to interview
  with City staff. The City’s selection committee evaluated and ranked the consultants in
  accordance with criteria stated in the RFP, which included compliance with RFP requirements,
  project understanding, experience and level of effort, schedule, and cost-effectiveness to
  provide efficient services. The proposal received from Hirsch & Associates, Inc., was ranked
  highest. As a High Park Need community, the City of Alhambra is eligible to receive Los
  Angeles County Regional Park and Open Space District Technical Assistance Program (TAP)
  funds for professional services and consulting resources. The professional engineering
  services for the design of the Alhambra Dog Park Project was an eligible use of TAP funds.

10.  AUTHORIZE SITE HOST AGREEMENT WITH EV CHARGING SOLUTIONS, INC., FOR
  THE REPLACEMENT OF EXISTING ELECTRIC VEHICLE CHARGING STATIONS AT
  THREE PARKING LOTS IN DOWNTOWN ALHAMBRA – F2M18-16, M2M24-141

  In November 2019, the City Council awarded a contract to EV Charging Solutions, Inc. (EVCS)
  to install eighteen (18) Level 2 EV charging stations. The EV charging stations were installed
  at 103 North Chapel Avenue; 26 North First Street; and 80 South First Street, with six chargers
  installed at each location. The existing equipment needed replacement and upgrade to newer,
  more efficient technology. EVCS prepared a new Site Host Agreement for the installation,
  operation and maintenance of the replacement EV charging stations. EVCS would be
  responsible for all material and labor costs associated with design, construction, maintenance,
  and operation of EV charging stations units, including electricity costs. Additionally, the
  agreement would generate revenue for the City at a rate of $0.05/kilowatt hour per charger,
  without incurring electricity costs by the City.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council authorized the City Manager, or designee, to execute a
  Site Host Agreement with EV Charging Solutions, Inc., to replace the existing electric vehicle
  (EV) charging stations at three parking lots in downtown Alhambra; and, directed staff to
  undertake the steps necessary to finalize the Council’s action. (M2M24-141)

  Ayes:  MALONEY, LEE, MAZA, ANDRADE-STADLER, PÉREZ

11.  CONTRACT AMENDMENT FOR TRAFFIC SCANNER CERTIFICATION TRAINING –
  F2M24-16, K2M23-378, M2M24-142

  In November 2023, after a competitive bidding process, a contract (K2M23-378) was issued
  to Faro Technologies, Inc. in the amount of $49,832.20 Faro Technologies, Inc. was a
  hardware and software company that provided 3D laser scanning solutions for crime scene
  reconstruction, traffic collision analysis and public safety operations. Staff requested to
  increase the contract by $15, 504 for the “Train the Trainer” program. The program was a
  five-day training course consisting of two Police Department employees trained to instruct
  future users on the operation of 3D scanning technology. Alhambra Police could then host
  classes to continue training employees and assist outside agencies that as use Faro 3D
  scanning systems.

12.  SECOND CONTRACT AMENDMENT: ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE ASSOCIATES –
F2M22-65, C2M23-64, M2M24-143

  On July 24, 2023, Environmental Science Associates (ESA) was awarded a contract for
  $145,000 to provide professional CEQA services for a Mitigated Negative Declaration (MND)
  analysis of the Alhambra Community Center Project. On September 11, 2023 the first
  amendment to ESA’s contract was necessary to revise the scope from an MND to a full
  Environmental Impact Report (“EIR”). The EIR’s studies and process required approximately
  1,000 additional professional hours and an extension of the entitlement schedule by
  approximately 30 weeks at a cost of an additional $215,219 in fees. A second contract
  amendment was necessary as a result of the initial study process, where it was determined
  that the EIR would also need to prepare studies, reports and an analysis of the following four
  additional CEQA issue areas: 1.) biological resources (special status species and wildlife
  corridors); 2.) cultural resources (archaeological resources); 3.) geology/soils (paleontological
  resources); 4.) tribal cultural resources (all thresholds). An additional $52,234 was required to
  conduct the additional analysis.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council approved a second amendment, subject to final language

  M2M24-160

  The Public Contract Code specified the procedures that public agencies must follow when
  they build public works projects, including limits on project costs. The California Uniform Public
  Construction Cost Accounting (CUPCCAA) Act was enacted in 1983 as an alternative to these
  general requirements by allowing increased bid limits as long as participating agencies follow
  uniform accounting standards and bidding procedures. Staff requested the City Council “opt
  in” to the provisions set forth by the CUPCCAA Act. This would allow public projects costing
  $60,000 or less to be performed by negotiated contract or by purchase order. Projects costing
  $200,000 or less could use informal bidding procedures set forth in the CUPCCAA Act.
  Projects that cost more than $200,000 must be put out to bid under formal bidding procedures.
  The benefits of adopting the CUPCCAA Act would increase the purchasing limit for public
  agencies, simplify bidding for projects that are $200,000 or less, reduce number of formal bids
  based on project size, and expedite contracting for projects under $200,000. In order for the
  City to avail itself of the higher bid and purchasing limits, the City must formally elect to be
  bound by the provisions of the Uniform Public Construction Cost Accounting Act, which
  specified the procedures for obtaining informal bids, and to use the uniform construction cost
  accounting procedures adopted by the California Uniform Construction Accounting
  Commission. Staff requested the City Council adopt Ordinance No. O2M24-4837 and update
  the City of Alhambra’s Purchasing Policy Limits as more specifically outlined in the Director of
  Finance’s August 26, 2024 staff report.

  City Attorney MONTES clarified the following points for revision in the ordinance: 1) Section
  3.40.030 the bonding requirements would remain at $25,000, and 2) Section 3.40.050 the
  retention would be 95%.
